title: Tom Hardy Is Officially Returning to ‘MobLand’ With Season 3 Renewal
full_text: Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 3, 2026 6:24am Pierce Brosnan, Helen Mirren and Tom Hardy lead 'MobLand.' Paramount+ Logo text Tom Hardy will remain with the MobLand cast for a third season — the official word was handed down on Thursday with a Paramount+ renewal. The streamer’s headline on its announcement: “THE HARRIGANS AREN’T GOING ANYWHERE.” That includes their fixer Harry da Souza, we now know for sure. MobLand also stars Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren as crime family patriarch and matriarch Conrad and Maeve Harrigan. Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Jasmine Jobson, Mandeep Dhillon, Geoff Bell, Daniel Betts, Janet McTeer, Jordi Mollà and Toby Jones star in supporting roles. Related Stories Movies Charlize Theron Reflects on 'Mad Max: Fury Road' a Decade Later: "There's a Deep Connection to This Film" TV 'Yellowjackets' Announces Final Season Premiere Date With Help From Kurt Loder MobLand season two is still weeks away from premiering — Friday, Sept. 18 — the early renewal is a vote of confidence in the series and a way to put the Hardy drama to bed. Hardy has been clashing with producers , THR reported in May, including executive producer Jez Butterworth and others at David Glasser’s 101 Studios, the production company behind MobLand , which is filmed across the U.K. “He refused to come out of his trailer for hours at a time,” the source says about Hardy’s on-set behavior on season two, which has spooked producers into rethinking Hardy’s future. The source adds: “He kept the cast waiting, [which is] a power play. Keeping Pierce Brosnan , Helen Mirren and others waiting is career suicide, I would wager.” Mad Max: Fury Road director George Miller and Star Trek: Nemesis actor Patrick Stewart have also discussed difficulties working with Hardy. In the upcoming MobLand season two, the Harrigans struggle to show a unified front as rising rivals threaten their fractured criminal empire. Da Souza, meanwhile, must walk a dangerous tightrope when tensions within the family intensify. As violence spills into every corner of their lives, loyalties snap, safety proves temporary, and the battle for power leaves no room for mercy. THR

title: Norah O’Donnell Returns to ‘CBS Mornings’ in Latest Network Shake Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 6:23am Norah O'Donnell Photo by Amy Sussman/Getty Images for Alliance for Women in Media Foundation CBS News is making another high-profile anchor change: The Bari Weiss-led network news division has named Norah O’Donnell co-host of its flagship morning program CBS Mornings . The new role will pair O’Donnell with Gayle King and Nate Burleson behind the anchor desk. It is also a homecoming for O’Donnell, who previously hosted the program from 2012-2019, before moving to the CBS Evening News . O’Donnell has been a senior correspondent and a frequent fill-in anchor since 2024 when her run at the evening newscast ended. She was also recently named a correspondent on 60 Minutes , where she was previously a contributor. Weiss has been reworking CBS News’ broadcast lineup, plucking Tony Dokoupil from the program for the Evening News slot, and most recently overhauling 60 Minutes under new executive producer Nick Bilton. The morning show has, by contrast, been more stable, with King inking a one-year deal this past spring. The return of O’Donnell will mark the beginning of the shows overhaul, even if it is a familiar one. Vlad Duthiers, Kelly O’Grady, and Adriana Diaz will continue to be daily contributors to the show, and the network is expected to add more names over the coming weeks. “This is a homecoming for Norah. As we all know, for seven years, Norah helped lead CBS This Morning alongside Gayle, creating one of the most memorable partnerships in the history of morning news,” CBS Mornings EP Jon Tower told staff in a memo Thursday morning. “They have a friendship and chemistry that extends beyond the studio. They know each other, respect each other, and — maybe most importantly — genuinely enjoy each other. To put it simply, I can’t think of a team I’d rather watch navigate the news than Gayle, Nate and Norah.” THR

title: Hollywood Veterans Launch aTwist Microdrama Platform With Horror, Comedy and Animated Series
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 6:05am The ‘Something Is Alive in My Attic’ horror microdrama from aTwist. Courtesy of aTwist The new microdramas platform from Hollywood veterans Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun has launched with an initial slate of projects spanning the horror, comedy and animation genres. On Thursday aTwist debuted in the U.S. and in seven other countries with the ambition to blend Hollywood-level storytelling with the twisty, addictive tropes of the burgeoning verticals format. The platform launched with 10 original series, including titles from The Bold and the Beautiful executive producer and head writer Bradley Bell and Abominable Pictures founder and Childrens Hospital executive producer Jonathan Stern. New series drop on Thursdays. Viewers can watch some episodes for free by viewing ads and can watch entire series by buying “coins” (a virtual currency) or buying an aTwist subscription. While romance stories currently dominate top vertical platforms, aTwist is launching with a mix of genres. One of its inaugural titles, Cash Out , is unscripted: It follows a woman on the mend from a broken relationship who is given $50,000 to spend in Vegas with her two best friends. Two titles, Something Is Alive in My Attic and Strangers, A Plane and a Deadly Game , are horror stories. I Fell in Love With the Dragon Prince , a fantasy-romance combo, is animated. There’s even a microdrama spoof series launching, from Abominable Pictures’ Stern, called My Billionaire Kidney . The logline? “A down-on-her-luck Cinderella-type becomes a pawn to her evil aunt and uncle and multiple absurdly powerful men as they fight for her kidney. Will she finally find a way to control the chaos and choose herself?” Soap opera veteran Bell, meanwhile, is behind a series called Hollywood Starlet , about a cleaner and aspiring actor who finally gets her shot at stardom when she attracts the romantic attentions of a well-known actor. The platform has been a while in the making. Winograde (the former president of Showtime), Rovner (previously the chairman of entertainment content at NBCUniversal Television and Streaming) and Braun (former chairman of WME) announced their venture in 2025, back when the company was called MicroCo. Since then, they’ve announced a creative partnership with Kevin Hart’s company Hartbeat, which will bring all of its microseries titles to aTwist. The platform has entered into a deal with BET to develop and distribute microdramas across linear and digital platforms and a pact with National CineMedia to advertise its series in movie theaters. THR

title: Inside Robert Pattinson’s Eerie Chris Hansen Transformation in ‘Primetime’: “A Reconfigured Egregore”
full_text: × Skip to main content 'Primetime' Courtesy of A24 For Lance Oppenheim , Primetime ’s DNA resides inside a silly Cameo video. The director, who’d grown up fascinated with To Catch a Predator ’s Chris Hansen , was celebrating the release of his FX documentary, 2024’s Spermworld , when his wife bought him a recorded message from the Dateline NBC host himself as a surprise gift. In it, Hansen congratulated Oppenheim on Spermworld , told him to “have a seat” — riffing on one of his beloved catchphrases from the series — and then, unusually, started pitching him on new projects he was working on. Related Stories Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering Movies 'Ink' Review: Jack O'Connell and Guy Pearce Trace Rupert Murdoch's Fleet Street Rise in Breathlessly Paced, Morally Opaque Danny Boyle Drama “I thought to myself, ‘Oh, he’s not just the crusading journalist, he’s also an entertainer, and he’s also self-aware of this media persona that he’s cultivated for a very long time,’” Oppenheim says. “That Cameo video almost crystallized the whole thing for me. In a weird way, this film is almost an adaptation of the Cameo video. He had been absorbed into this strange, performative version of himself.” Watch Primetime , which stars Robert Pattinson as Hansen, and that vision is clear. The film, loosely adapted by first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh from an Esquire article by Luke Dittrich, dramatizes the darkest year in Hansen’s time on To Catch a Predator , which ran from 2004-07 and saw the host trapping would-be pedophiles in hidden-camera setups before often coordinating their arrest with law enforcement. The show was a phenomenon that continues to inspire copycats and parodies; Hansen emerged as an icon for some, and a meme for others. Tony Revolori and Robert Pattinson in ‘Primetime.’ Primetime plays directly into that. This is anything but an authorized biopic. Oppenheim describes his approach as “docufantasia,” and indeed, Primetime is best experienced as a probing, darkly surreal immersion into the mid-aughts, and specifically the era’s rapidly transforming media landscape that allowed Hansen to evolve from broadcast journalist to “mythological being,” in Oppenheim’s words. “I always loved the way To Catch a Predator mixed truth and fiction — creating this apparatus, blending artifice actors with fake decoy houses and props like the sweet tea and the pepperoni pizza, that would then collide with very, very real stakes,” Oppenheim says. “How do you create something that captures the darkest feelings of humanity mixed with the feeling you would get when you’d hear Chris Hansen say one of his all-time great one-liners?” Primetime will premiere at the Venice Film Festival in just a few days. Hansen was not involved in the making of the movie, a conscious choice on the part of the filmmakers, and has already spoken out against it in various ways. He questioned “Hollywood’s motive” in making the movie. He suggested Denis Leary would’ve been a better casting choice than Pattinson. He lambasted studio A24 for being asked “to sign away my rights to my name” after being presented with a nondisclosure agreement in advance of a screening of the film; he declined to sign, and therefore has still not seen the movie. (A source close to A24 says that the document he was asked to sign was a standard NDA for the studio’s pre-premiere screenings.) Pattinson and Skyler Gisondo in ‘Primetime.’ Sinna Nasseri “It’s the first time I’ve ever thought I could say this — I’m excited for him to ‘have a seat’ and watch the movie in a movie theater, if that’s where he chooses to watch it,” Oppenheim says cheekily. “I hope, when the time comes, that he sees it — and I’m excited to hear what he has to say about it.” When pressed on Hansen’s claims that he felt he was being asked to sign away his legal rights via the NDA, the director adds: “I can’t really speak to that because I wasn’t there when that all happened, but I know — and I hope he knows — that this film is an exploration of what this kind of work does to the people who make it. It’s based on and inspired by the experiences of working inside an extremely dark world 24/7, attempting to do extremely serious journalism, and how that becomes also extremely confusing when you’re tasked with turning it into an entertaining television show.” *** Pattinson was in his late teens during To Catch a Predator ’s run, but caught on once he came to the U.S. in his early 20s, at the dawn of his Twilight fame. “I had no idea how massive the viewership was when it came out. I first watched reruns of the show on a channel that used to play back-to-back episodes for what felt like all day,” he says. “It was not just the intensely serious subject that the show is about that was connecting to a huge audience. It was something more.” Singh felt that way too. “I was not really interested in a biopic,” the screenwriter says. “I wanted to create something heightened, stylized and subjective, dancing on the line between reality and spectacle, which To Catch a Predator did so well.” His script met a “sobering” marketplace, where few would even read it due to its challenging subject matter. In a lucky break, it eventually wound up in the hands of Pattinson and Brighton McCloskey, who were just ramping up their Icki Eneo Arlo producing banner. They were interested instantly. Pattinson had known and followed Oppenheim’s work for years, and after looping him in, everything came together quickly. Pattinson in ‘Primetime.’ The director, writer and producers jointly executed a plan to mount Primetime over long talks. “A big part of those early stages was trying to convince Rob to act in the film instead of solely producing,” Singh says. Indeed, Pattinson had a pretty full plate. Primetime marks his first producing credit — “It was the first time I’ve been on a project pre-director through release,” he says. “I was prepping Primetime while shooting Die My Love and The Drama .” He then started filming on The Odyssey only “a day after wrap” on Primetime : “Trying to prep The Odyssey while shooting Primetime was a bit more difficult,” he admits. So what convinced him to squeeze the role into his relentless schedule? The character — specifically, the version realized by Oppenheim and Singh — proved too compelling for the chameleonic star to resist. “There was something in the design of the show and the alchemy [of] what Chris Hansen was doing that was creating something entirely unpredictable,” Pattinson says. “I was interested in finding out what that was. As I continued to investigate, I became increasingly interested in playing a character who was trying to figure out what that ineffable alchemy was, in real time, while simultaneously becoming unexpectedly, incredibly famous. “I watched a ton of the show, every episode of his podcast, every interview I could find,” Pattinson continues. “But I knew from the first read of the script that the character in the movie was going to be a conceptual figure based on the public persona of ‘Chris Hansen’ as he’s been portrayed and perceived across all mediums and internet culture — a reconfigured egregore of sorts.” The filmmakers couldn’t have anticipated how that notion would materialize on set. Pattinson arrived with an eerie approximation of Hansen’s voice — Hansen himself conceded it was a “pretty good imitation” from viewing the trailer — and, more deeply, a kind of physiological transformation that would define Primetime ’s very aesthetic. Once Oppenheim saw what his star was up to, he realized he didn’t have to veer too much from his approach on his docs — a fact only bolstered by much of Oppenheim’s crew from his recent projects, like HBO’s Ren Faire , returning for Primetime . “Every day Rob would come in and would do something that felt like he was almost jumping off a cliff — make a decision or a choice that was so unexpected and so inspired that I wanted to engage with him how I normally would with a documentary subject,” the director says. “I gave him a lot of rope and allowed for his performance and his choices to dictate the tone of the film — which in some ways is exactly how Chris Hansen in the television show would go about things.” Oppenheim adds of Pattinson’s performance, “he stitched very vulnerable parts of himself with every version of Chris Hansen that’s ever existed that we’ve ever seen. … We consumed every single thing about him out there and, somehow, what Rob’s performance is to me is a media collage of this cultural mythology that Chris Hansen has created.” Lance Oppenheim on the set of ‘Primetime.’ Sinna Nasseri Primetime also features rich performances from Merritt Wever as Hansen’s dogged producer and, in a true breakout, Skyler Gisondo as “Decoy” Dan Plumb, an aspiring young (adult) actor who’s cast to pose as a minor to help lure in predators for the show. (He’s a composite character who shares the first name of Dan Schrack, a real Predator decoy who was involved in a tragic incident depicted in both the Esquire article and in Primetime .) “I didn’t feel like I was the kind of actor who was considered for roles like this,” says Gisondo, known for his comic work in Booksmart and the upcoming Focker-in-Law . Dan emerges as Primetime ’s unlikely heart, bewildered by the dark world he’s wandered into and left to negotiate his ambitions with the high stakes of the job. “My own personal nervousness bled into it,” Gisondo says. “The very first take of the first scene of the first day, I remember watching Rob, thinking, ‘This is the best acting I’ve ever seen in my life.’ You’re having this experience of trying to just do your thing, but you can’t help but be in awe of his thing — and to a degree, that’s what is going on between Dan and Chris, since Dan is awe-struck by Chris.” *** Gisondo came of age as a child actor, and drew from his early experiences in the industry to bring palpable complexity to Dan. The dramatized nature of Primetime leads to other inspired casting choices — like Phoebe Bridgers , who makes her acting debut as a fellow decoy, in this case a young woman tasked with portraying both boys and girls on Predator . Bridgers has known Oppenheim since long before becoming a famous musician. “I’ve always known her to have an incredibly deep, almost baritone speaking voice, and I was then amazed that someone who had such a deep speaking voice could produce this beautiful, angelic singing voice,” Oppenheim says. “With how she’s able to use her voice in different environments, I kept thinking, ‘That’s exactly what a decoy would do.’ I remember texting her like, ‘This is so random, but I think you are perfect for this part,’ and she responded, ‘I don’t really act, I’ve never done it, I don’t know how.’ ” He convinced her that she did. Gisondo in ‘Primetime.’ The most surprising appearance of all, however, is that of longtime media executive Jeff Zucker, tearing into a boorish version of himself. In 2006, Zucker oversaw programming across all of NBCUniversal, including To Catch a Predator , and we see him in bizarro-world action in Primetime . He instructs Chris to devise ways of blowing To Catch a Predator up to meet the insatiable demand — going so far as to risk programming it against Lost . Zucker spoke with Oppenheim on background before agreeing to play himself. “He gave me such great information and texture for the time period and what was going on, what the slate was like at NBC,” Oppenheim says. “I loved the idea, keeping with the project of making this a true fever dream, of having real people alongside actors, but I wasn’t sure if Jeff would want to do it.” Zucker agreed, though, and has since watched and approved of the film. “He really enjoyed it,” Oppenheim says. “I’m very honored that he did it, in playing a version of himself that was the driver of tasking Chris Hansen and his team to think of the show as a commercial object.” Zucker’s presence does more than nod to the period, however — it speaks to one of Primetime ’s most potent ideas, the outrageous collision of journalism and entertainment. “We became increasingly interested in the dichotomies in the show,” Pattinson says. “The sharp splits between reality and artifice, between the shockingly serious and the absurd.” Oppenheim sees To Catch a Predator on a continuum that’s lasted thousands of years. “This TV show was a form of performative justice. We used to have the pillory, we used to have whipping posts, and the new incarnations of it, on TikTok and elsewhere, are forms of that,” he says. “It’s ingrained in our DNA to want this spectacle of justice.” Minute to minute, Primetime will make you feel many things — it’ll force you to question reality, bring you up agonizingly close to an unknowable figure, submerge you in the choppy waters of an infamous TV show’s methods. It may not, however, leave you with a feeling of justice being served. “Right now, more than maybe ever, it feels like that conversation and that desire is very much alive in our culture,” Oppenheim says. “So I’m excited to see what kind of conversations this film creates.” THR

title: The Fix Is Not In: Can Sports Gambling’s Trust Crisis Be Solved?
full_text: × Skip to main content By Andrew Zucker Plus Icon Andrew Zucker View All September 3, 2026 6:00am Layer Ø Lanny Brannock lives just outside Lexington, Kentucky, which makes him partial to Cincinnati sports . And as the co-host of a podcast in which he wagers tiny sums on sporting events, he is hyper-engaged on outcomes. It just isn’t always as a sports superfan. “It does take some of the joy out of watching the game,” he says. “You’re not just watching it for the sheer athletic ability anymore because you’re financially involved.” Brannock has no plans to stop betting, but thanks to a wave of recent athlete gambling scandals, he’s growing concerned about the integrity of the onscreen product — and what it means for sports. Related Stories Business Another California Sports Team Sold As Stan Kroenke Cuts Deal to Buy Los Angeles Angels TV Where to Watch the 2026 U.S. Open Tennis Tournament Online “If you start to lose a segment of your fan base because people believe with some reasoned certainty that there are predetermined outcomes, or players are going into business for themselves, then it will hurt sports overall,” he tells me. While the sports industrial complex has largely been immune from America’s trust crisis, new concerns over betting’s influence on game integrity are not only worrying fans like Brannock, but also league officials. “It’s on everybody’s mind,” says John Kosner, a former ESPN executive. Each of the United States’ four biggest leagues — the NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL — has investigated its personnel for suspicious betting activity in the past 12 months, causing some spectators to consider whether sports are morphing into WrestleMania. “The nightmare scenario for the leagues is that people see professional sports as professional wrestling,” says Jonathan D. Cohen, the author of Losing Big: America’s Reckless Bet on Sports Gambling . Plenty of people still watch WWE, even after Vince McMahon had to admit its staging in 1989, but its revenues are dwarfed by rival three-letter leagues. That’s because content companies are willing to shell out major bucks to air live, anything-can-happen matches, which tend to draw bigger audiences than scripted fare. But fans’ growing distrust of airtight competition could threaten to puncture sky-high media rights. NBC News found that 70 percent of Americans believe betting “lessens the integrity of the game,” according to the December poll . Meanwhile, a recent Ipsos poll revealed that almost half of all Americans are concerned that games are “rigged” due to betting. It’s contributed to the rise of a police force for sportsbooks. There are now a number of betting monitoring companies eagle-eyed on spotting suspicious wagers. Integrity Compliance 360 is one of the biggest in the space. In 2023, IC360, as it’s also known, cut a deal with UFC to identify shady bets. “These guys are really good at seeing weird betting patterns, and they literally reach out to you and say, ‘Hey, there’s some goofy stuff going on with this fight,’” UFC impresario Dana White told CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin in July. White dialed the FBI in November after his company hosted a potentially rigged fight in which Isaac Dulgarian, the cage match’s favorite, lost by first-round submission. Dulgarian was subsequently suspended by the Nevada State Athletic Commission. Isaac Dulgarian (left) battled Christian Rodriguez in their featherweight fight during the UFC Fight Night event at UFC APEX on March 16, 2024, in Las Vegas. Dulgarian lost in the first round, leading to accusations that he took a dive. Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC/Getty Images One of IC360’s most popular products is ProhiBet, which launched in 2023. It offers secure transfer of a list of prohibited bettors from sports leagues (think: players, coaches, even equipment managers) to betting sites. That allows companies such as Caesars Sportsbook, which uses the product, as well as leagues to stamp out potential corruption in games. Of course, there are ways to circumvent cybercops. Athletes could use offshore sportsbooks, for example, or have others place bets on their behalf. But organizers such as the PGA Tour and NCAA are using the IC360 tool as a means to at least reduce the chances of corruption. One of the biggest threats to sports integrity stems from prop betting, which allows for betting on non-final-score events, such as an athlete’s free-throw percentage or number of receptions. These types of wagers have grown alongside the rise of prediction markets, which constantly spin up micro-event contracts. “If you’re a sports commissioner, you might want to see them eliminated or really sort of buttoned up more vigorously,” says Kosner of same-game parlays, which often involve multiple prop bets in one game. It’s often these small-event wagers driving unfortunate headlines. Emmanuel Clase, a baseball closer who pitched for the Cleveland Guardians, reportedly rigged individual pitches across three seasons. He is facing trial later this year. Terry Rozier, who played for the Charlotte Hornets, allegedly faked an injury in 2023 to leave a game early in order to benefit “under” prop bettors. He is scheduled to face trial next year. Jontay Porter, who played for the Toronto Raptors, was banned for life from the NBA for placing bets on himself. Cleveland Guardians relief pitcher Emmanuel Clase is facing trial for allegedly rigging pitches across three seasons in an attempt to illicitly profit from so-called prop bets. Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images These granular event contracts are different from betting scandals of yore, when athletes like former Reds player Pete Rose and ex-NBA referee Tim Donaghy — to say nothing of the notorious Chicago “Black” Sox of 1919 — benefited from mostly betting on final outcomes, not player performances. They also mean more athletes have the opportunity to make serious dough betting on their efforts. “The line you hear from gambling companies all the time is like, ‘Oh, we need to offer all this stuff because it’s already being offered in the illegal market,” says Cohen. “I don’t think anyone in the illegal market was gambling on Jontay Porter under rebounds.” Whether fans end up growing frustrated with integrity issues or not, gambling still threatens to morph devoted fandoms into dispassionate audiences. “I think this whole thing is just a Faustian bargain for the sports leagues, where in the short term it’s driving interest in their product, and maybe is increasing their media rights deals,” adds Cohen. “But over the long term, you’re not creating NBA fans. You’re just creating a bunch of people who like gambling on the NBA, and they might as well be gambling on Malaysian badminton.” Jontay Porter, formerly of Toronto Raptors, was banned for life from the NBA for placing bets on himself. Mark Blinch/Getty Images This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s August 2026 Sports issue .

title: Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago
full_text: Sep 3, 2026 6:00am PT Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty 20 minutes ago ‘60 Minutes’ Faces New Challenge After Off-Season Chaos: Getting Back on the Air 18 hours ago Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Fox News Steve Doocy and Brian Kilmeade are preparing for a reunion of sorts that neither is eager to remember. On September 11, 2001, both Fox News Channel personalities were working on air as news organizations throughout the New York area were trying to cover devastating attacks by terrorists on the two massive skyscrapers at the World Trade Center. “It has always been a very sober and somber day on ‘Fox & Friends,’” Doocy says of the anniversary of 9/11 . “We were there from the beginning. It’s just one of those days where you sit up a little straighter because of the gravity of the day.” Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ For Kilmeade, the day marked a turning point in his career at Fox News, because he was dispatched to get to downtown Manhattan and capture what was happening. “Keep in mind I was hired for sports. I was always doing sports on the morning show,” he recalls. But after a surreal trip downtown with crew members, he says, “they no longer thought of me as a sports guy after that. I certainly didn’t think of myself as that.” Popular on Variety Next week, “Fox & Friends” will spend time remembering the tragedy around the 25 th anniversary of its occurrence. Doocy will host the morning program’s “Breakfast with Friends” series live from O’Hara’s Pub in downtown Manhattan just two blocks from Ground Zero. Doocy will on Tuesday travel to Washington, D.C. and speak with Tunnels to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller. On Thursday, Doocy will broadcast live from Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93. And on Friday, September 11th, Fox News Channel’s special coverage will commence with “Fox & Friends co-hosts Kilmeade, Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones broadcasting live from the Hyatt House in Jersey City, overlooking the New York City skyline, while Doocy will contribute live from Ground Zero. Other programs will also nod to the anniversary. “America’s Newsroom” will carry the live reading of the victims’ names from the National September 11 Memorial & Museum. Martha MacCallum, host of “The Story,” will feature an interview with Cardinal Timothy Dolan, the New York Police Department co-chief chaplain, and another with NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. Fox News’ efforts will join those of ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, MS NOW and CNN. The 25th anniversary of the attacks has spurred many news organizations to offer a broader array of programming, which in most years is largely tied to comemmoration. Many journalists had to pivot on 9/11, moving from traditional morning-news programming to rolling crisis coverage. Not many of them remain on active duty. Kilmeade still has vivid recollections of his time visiting Ground Zero on the actual day planes crashed into the two World Trade Center towers. “People were blown out of their shoes,” he remembers. “You could not see the ground. It felt like you were on the moon.” He remembers handing in tapes of what he and the Fox News crew assigned to him had collected, “and I’ve never seen them since.” In a sign of how unexpected the attacks were, Doocy was, before chaos erupted, tending to something entirely different for the Fox News morning program. “I was outside I was doing the weather with Mr. Peanut,” he remembers. “Planters Peanuts has that mascot. I’m interviewing Mr. Peanut,” which presented some challenges. After all, says Doocy, “Mr. Peanut doesn’t talk.” When he walked 15 feet back into the studio, people were on alert. There was a report of a plane crashing into one of the World Trade Center towers, but there was not much detail. “Nobody had any images,” recalls Doocy. There was speculation that a helicopter or small plane had gone off course. From there, both Doocy and Kilmeade remember hours of work and of staying in different hotel rooms in New York after the city closed access. Doocy didn’t see his family for two days. Fox News Media on September 11 will provide coverage and commemoration throughout the day. Eric Shawn, a Fox News Channel senior correspondent who reported from Ground Zero in 2001, will be on hand to provide coverage. At Fox Business Network, Liz Claman, anchor of “The Claman Countdown,” will speak with Brandon and Kyle Lutnick, the Chairman and Executive Vice Chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, on September 10th and on September 11, will interview Larry Silverstein, founder and CEO of Silverstein Properties, from the World Trade Center, which he helped rebuild. Streaming outlet Fox Nation will debut two new specials exploring the impact of the 9/11 attacks 25 years later. Doocy hopes such work will ensure Americans remember the terrible day, no matter the memories and feelings it sparks. With the event a quarter century old, he wonders if “the day has lost its potency for a lot of people, its place in history.” The news business employs many young producers, he notes, “who weren’t alive at the time.” The work being done next week by a broad array of news organizations will try to keep remembrances of the day active. title: AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion
full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:59am PT AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion 27 minutes ago YouTube Travel Creator Drew Binsky Inks Netfix Deal 21 hours ago Apple TV Inks Deal With Yahoo Sports for Free Alt-Casts of MLS Matches and MLB Games (but Only the First Two Innings) 1 day ago See All Getty Images Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang is making a big new bet on an open-source AI future. On Thursday, Huang announced that Nvidia, a major supplier of hardware to power AI applications, reached a deal to acquire Hugging Face — which operates a platform for building AI open-source models — for $12.93 billion. “Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide,” Huang wrote in a blog post. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf in New York City. More than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover, evaluate, customize and deploy AI, according to the company. Popular on Variety The company was also the subject of an attack by rogue OpenAI agents in July that saw the agents break out of a controlled testing environment, access the internet and hack parts of Hugging Face’s internal systems. The incident, along with subsequent episodes disclosed by Anthropic and Meta, sparked an industry-wide push to slow development of frontier AI models to improve safeguards to keep autonomous agents under human control. Hugging Face will “remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” Huang said. “Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want.” He added that Nvidia systems will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face. “Hugging Face will continue to support open source and open weight models from across the ecosystem, from every model builder. It will continue to support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment, so builders can use the hardware and infrastructure that best fit their work,” Huang wrote. Huang recently coauthored an open letter on the importance of open weights to the AI economy. “Joined by leaders from across the industry, we made a simple point: open weights broaden access to AI and help ensure that AI leadership is distributed across companies, institutions and communities,” he wrote. “Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch. They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job. That is how AI can advance safely, strengthen cybersecurity and sovereignty, accelerate innovation, and reach factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms and Main Street businesses around the world,” Huang said. “AI advances faster when people can build together.” To date, Nvidia has been the largest contributor of open models and data to Hugging Face. According to Huang, Nvidia has released more than 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue told CNBC that his company approached Huang about a deal a few weeks ago. “During the summer, I think we realized that Hugging Face and open source AI in general was at the turning point, and that it needed more, more resources, more scale, more visibility,” he said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” How ‘A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,’ ‘Fallout’ and ‘Spider-Noir’ Production Designers Built Out Their Worlds While Honoring the Source Material ‘Tony’ Star Dominic Sessa on How Being a ‘Liar’ Helped Him Portray Anthony Bourdain and Why the Film Foreshadows His Later Struggles After the YA Drama ‘Sterling Point’ Topped the Prime Video Charts, What’s Next for LuckyChap TV? title: Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty
full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:55am PT Norah O’Donnell, On Rise at CBS News, Returns to Morning Duty By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago 26 minutes ago ‘60 Minutes’ Faces New Challenge After Off-Season Chaos: Getting Back on the Air 18 hours ago Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea 2 days ago See All Michele Crowe/CBS Norah O’Donnell is back in a place where many people feel she always belonged — as one of the top anchors of CBS News . On Tuesday, A.M. viewers will see O’Donnell alongside Gayle King and Nate Burleson on “ CBS Mornings ,” in a new trio that CBS News executives believe will stabilize the program’s ratings and give viewers more of a reason to watch. O’Donnell is rejoining CBS’ morning program after leaving in May of 2019 to take up a role as the anchor of “CBS Evening News.” Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ “We believe there is a lot of life left in morning television, and therefore we are putting our best people on the field,” says Tom Cibrowski, the president of CBS News, in an interview. “People have very serious issues to deal with every day in their lives, and between Norah, Gayle and Nate, the three of them bring relatability, credibility. experience and knowledge, and they are incredibly familiar to CBS viewers, which is important.” Popular on Variety O’Donnell previously co-anchored the CBS morning program with King and Charlie Rose, starting in 2012, and helped the show gain the kind of traction CBS has not often seen in that time period. She returns at a crucial moment. CBS has long come in third behind NBC’s “Today” and ABC’s “Good Morning America,” but in recent months has seen its standing in early news slip further. Season to date as of August 30, the overall “CBS Mornings” has fallen about 9% from the year-earlier period to approximately 1.7 million, according to figures from Nielsen. Both “Today” and “GMA” enjoy viewership of just under 3 million and have seen their audiences increase. The standing of “CBS Mornings” among people between 25 and 54, the crowd most coveted by advertisers in news programming, is eroding noticeably — down 20% from a year ago, to about 278,000 viewers. “Today” is off 2% to 612,000 while “GMA” is up 2% to 478,000. O’Donnell, represented by UTA, may restore an element to the morning show that it hasn’t had in some time. King and Burleson stand as strong journalists and winning on-screen personalities, but O’Donnell brings a set of hard-news credentials that are hard to match. O’Donnell has investigated harassment in the U.S. armed forces and snared a hard-to-get interview with Pope Francis. In a sign of the new value she holds at CBS News, O’Donnell is also joining “60 Minutes” as a correspondent and recently launched a podcast centered on women’s health. “All of that experience and energy makes her a perfect match for Gayle and Nate,” says Jon Tower, the producer overseeing ‘CBS Mornings,” in a memo sent to staff Thursday. “Gayle is one of the hardest-working and best interviewers in the business, with an unmatched ability to connect with audiences on all topics. And Nate brings curiosity, warmth, spontaneity and a perspective that can take a conversation in a direction none of us expected.” O’Donnell’s arrival at “Mornings” is only one of several new developments viewers will see at the show. Look for “CBS Mornings” to tamp down some of the feature segments it shows and instead dive into live discussions on important topics, says Cibrowski, who wants to bring more “in-the-moment” discussions tied to the news cycle. O’Donnell and anchor Kelly O’Grady recently led a segment tied to the current trial of Lindsay Clancy, who maintains she suffered from postpartum psychosis, which played a role in her strangulation of her three children. “It was an incredibly engaging segment — informational and authentic,” says Cibrowski. “That’s the direction we want to be in. We want to be, first and foremost, informative and helpful to the core audience that’s watching morning television.” He also expects both King and O’Donnell to book important newsmakers from a wide variety of fields for revealing interviews. “These two work non-stop to make stuff happen,” he says. When asked how soon viewers would start seeing more of these kinds of segments, Cibrowski replied, “Very quickly.” Cibrowski has had prior success with morning TV. He has also logged time as a senior executive at ABC News, where he was among those who helped boost “Good Morning America” over NBC’s “Today” for the first time in years. Cibrowski was executive producer of the show when it flipped the morning-TV hierarchy. CBS News is seeking other personalities for the A.M., the executive says. “We are absolutely engaged in looking for more permanent on-air contributors, whether they be in lifestyle or health or other things that impact people.” But it is O’Donnell who will inject a new presence at the program starting next week. She has popped up on “CBS Mornings” in recent weeks as CBS News has looked at chemistry among various hosts and guests. Elisabeth Hasselbeck and Eva Pilgrim are among the others who have been seen. O’Donnell has since January of 2025 worked as a senior correspondent at CBS News, contributing to a variety of programs at CBS News. There are many who feel CBS News might be in a better position had previous management kept her in the anchor chair in the evening. CBS News decided to experiment with an evening format that featured two anchors — John Dickerson and Maurice DuBois — with a focus on enterprise storytelling. There were good intentions behind the concept, but a chunk of viewers left the program — and have not come back. Now O’Donnell has a new chance to give the audience, albeit one in a different time slot, something exciting to watch. full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:44am PT Paolo Strippoli on His Venice Thriller ‘The Spiral’ and Directing Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a Demonic Character Who Does ‘Truly Horrible Things’ (EXCLUSIVE) Watch the first clip from the film below By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Paolo Strippoli on His Venice Thriller ‘The Spiral’ and Directing Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a Demonic Character Who Does ‘Truly Horrible Things’ (EXCLUSIVE) 33 minutes ago Danny Boyle Celebrated at Variety’s Venice Pre-Opening Party as ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell Praises His Ability to ‘Take Us Inside a World’ 23 hours ago Francesco Carrozzini on His Venice AI Doc ‘Be Brave’ and Why ‘The Human Has to Come First’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Courtesy Filmitalia Paolo Strippoli , who is Italy’s hottest young helmer of genre movies, is back at Venice Film Festival with “ The Spiral .” The high-concept thriller stars Valeria Bruni Tedeschi as a demonic character called The Stranger, who entices a young mother played by Jasmine Trinca into forging a Faustian pact. “The Spiral” centers on a mother-daughter relationship that spirals out of control following a shocking revelation. At the film’s start, a woman named Anna suddenly shows up at her daughter’s Alice’s house during a thunderstorm saying she wants to tell her a dark truth about their family. She claims to have made a pact with The Stranger to save Alice’s leg after an accident 20 years earlier. That pact “has triggered a domino effect causing terrible events over the years. Only Alice can help to put everything right. But at what price?” the synopsis says. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Besides Tedeschi and Trinca, “The Spiral” cast also comprises Romana Maggiora Vergano (“There’s Still Tomorrow”) and Adriano Giannini (“Supersex”). The film was lead produced by Rome-based Propaganda in tandem with France’s Kazak Productions. Popular on Variety Strippoli made his directorial debut in 2021 with “A Classic Horror Story,” a hit Netflix Original film he co-directed with Roberto De Feo. In 2022, he helmed his second feature, the psychological horror “Piove.” And in 2025, Strippoli’s third movie, “The Holy Boy” launched from Venice. Below, Strippoli speaks to Variety about working with his top-notch cast on “The Spiral” and reveals an exclusive clip from the film. How did this story originate? “The Spiral” was born as a novel that I wanted to write. Then, when I told this story to my co-screenwriter, Salvatore De Chirico, he said, “Let’s make it into a film.” It was born from my fear of not having control over things in life. It’s a film about control, about how it’s impossible to determine our destiny. We live in a society, in a world that teaches us and pushes us to self-determination. But the truth is that self-determination is not always possible. Would you say this is a film about motherhood or, more broadly, parenthood? One of the themes is parenthood and a way of conceiving motherhood and parental love as control and ambition that is projected onto one’s children. Not that Anna Colonna or Walter Colonna, the parents in this family, are evil, They are certainly overbearing personalities, but they are not bad people. I have never seen them as people who don’t truly love their children. Simply, they are a product of the society in which they live, the city of Bari at the end of the last century, a time of great industrial and economic growth. What we see are these rich people who are social climbers with new money after having achieved a certain social status. But they were not born into that social class. Talk to me about working with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, who plays the role of The Stranger? She’s an amazing actress and also very generous on set. First of all, I want to say that it was very easy to convince Valeria to do this film, maybe also because the role was written for her. I couldn’t imagine anyone other than Valeria Bruni Tedeschi in the role of The Stranger. Because in this film, Valeria does truly horrible things, but she does it with a lightness that is also very funny. Sometimes she makes you laugh, but it never takes away from the cruelty of what she is saying. I think Valeria is one of the few Italian actresses — even though she’s an international actress, she lives in France and works in France —who has this quality of never judging the things she says. They are always suspended in time and tone. Talk to me about casting Jasmine Trinca as Anna Colonna, in what is an unusual role for her. We wrote the script with Jasmine in mind, but she was harder to convince than Valeria. It took us years, and now she laughs about this. I didn’t want any other actress, even though everyone who read the script was like, “I love Jasmine Trinca to bits, but it’s not a role I expect from her.” Why was Jasmine Trinca perfect to play Anna Colonna and what indications did you give her? Because Jasmine is deeply empathetic, almost sweet, even when she does and says mean things in movies. She has an empathetic quality that always makes you feel for her, that makes you always love her. It’s because she’s an actress and a person of great emotional intelligence. As for my indications, even though she always keeps her acting naturalistic, we worked on making it clear what type of mother Anna is: her rigidity, her control. We worked on achieving this. Anna is a character who could easily be labeled unpleasant, mean and evil. But the way she is played by Jasmine, she is a mother who — in her own twisted, sick and sometimes perverse way — wants the best for her children and the best for her family. Do you consider this a horror film? No. I never conceived of this as a horror film. For me, it’s always been a psychological thriller; a puzzle that comes together as the film progresses. Obviously, it plays with the tropes of horror films, a genre that I love deeply and am very familiar with. But over time, I think I’ve figured this out: definitions of the category or the genres of a film should be given by the people who see it: by the [industry] professionals, by critics and journalists and by the audience. My job was to tell this story in an honest and entertaining way. So, I never thought about the specific genre of this film. I just thought it should be an exciting journey for the viewer, obviously. Then, when I saw the film for myself, this confirmed to me that it’s not a horror film. Once I assembled it and I started editing it, and got the complete, overall vision of what I’d done, I saw that it definitely went in the direction of a psychological thriller. Because it’s a film that works on twists and turns, on revelations. It’s a puzzle, where the last little piece arrives in the final shot of the film. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. title: Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 3, 2026 5:36am PT Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Lesley Manville Takes on Cold War Poland in ‘Winter of the Crow’ Trailer as Cohen Sets Thriller’s U.S. Release Date (EXCLUSIVE) 43 minutes ago Jeff Goldblum to Host ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2 Premiere 3 hours ago See-Saw Films Taps Fifth Season’s Ben Irving for Joint Managing Director Role as Helen Gregory Steps Down From ‘Slow Horses’ Banner 4 hours ago See All Courtesy of SSIFF Lesley Manville battles snow and spies in the trailer for upcoming Cold War thriller “ Winter of the Crow ,” from director Kasia Adamik and set against the turmoil of 1981 Warsaw. Alongside releasing the official trailer, Cohen Media Group has also announced that the film will release theatrically nationwide on Oct 9. Inspired by Nobel Prize-winning author Olga Tokarczuk’s highly acclaimed “Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw,” “Winter of the Crows” stars Manville as Joan Andrews, a British psychiatry professor who travels to Warsaw in December 1981 as a guest lecturer at a local university. When Martial Law is suddenly imposed and the country shuts down overnight, Joan finds herself trapped in an increasingly dangerous and unfamiliar world. Related Stories Grammys May Reconsider New Asian Pop Award After BTS Withdrawal: ‘Some Artists Feel This Category Isn’t Representing the Music They Create’ Armed with her Polaroid camera, Joan witnesses a brutal murder by the secret police. With Poland effectively sealed off and her own life now in danger, she is forced into hiding and becomes a hunted fugitive, navigating a city transformed by fear, political repression and violence. Popular on Variety Alongside Manville, an Oscar nominee who recently won a Tony award for her role the revival of Greek tragedy, “Oedipus,” the cast includes Tom Burke (“Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga,” “The Souvenir”), Andrzej Konopka (“The Lure,” “Nina”),Sascha Ley (“We’ll Find Happiness”) and Zofia Wichłacz (“World on Fire”). In its review of the film, Variety praised the performance of Manville, saying she “carries the film with an air of increasingly raw determination.” “Anchored by a remarkable performance from Lesley Manville, Kasia Adamik has created a film that is both a gripping thriller and a deeply human story,” said Robert Aaronson, executive vice president of Cohen Media Group. “The screenplay truly captures the uncertainty and tension of this pivotal moment in history. We’re very proud to bring it to theaters this October.” Added Adamik: “’Winter of the Crow’ is deeply personal to me, and I wanted to capture the fear and uncertainty of a moment when everyday life could change in an instant. Lesley Manville brings such intelligence, strength and humanity to Joan, and I’m thrilled that audiences will have the opportunity to experience her extraordinary performance—and this story—on the big screen.” The film was produced by Olga Chajdas, Stanisław Dziedzic, Katarzyna Ozga, Nicolas Steil and Samantha Taylor, and adapted from the short story by Tokarczuk. The film was co-financed by the Polish Film Institute, Film Fund Luxembourg, UK Global Screen Fund and Silesia Film. Agnieszka Holland serves as executive producer. title: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Canters Into The Awards Race With John Malkovich Leading The Charge — Venice Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Sony Sets Release Date For Indian Epic ‘Ramayana’ With Ranbir Kapoor, Yash & Sai Pallavi ‘Ink’: What The Critics Are Saying About Danny Boyle’s Origin Story Of Brit Tabloid The Sun Javier Bardem, Marion Cotillard & Vanessa Redgrave Join Animated Movie ‘The Turning Door’ View All September 3, 2026 5:36am VENICE, ITALY - SEPTEMBER 03: (L-R) John Malkovich, Mariana Di Girolamo, Parker Posey, Director Martin McDonagh, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, and Ailín Salas attend the "Wild Horse Nine" Photocall during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival at Palazzo del Casino on September 03, 2026 in Venice, Italy. (Photo by Daniele Venturelli/WireImage) Getty Martin McDonagh ‘s Wild Horse Nine launched on the Lido this morning with the filmmakers and cast getting a rapturous welcome at the press conference following this morning’s press screenings. Venice pressers tend to fall on the warm/adulating side but this was clearly a film with plenty of admirers. Director Martin McDonagh, and actors John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi and Parker Posey were among those up on stage to discuss the dark comedy, whose Oscar buzz has been building. The presser got underway with a journalist telling the team that the film was one of the best he’d seen this year and that Malkovich could surely start writing his Oscar acceptance speech, noting that it would be the accolade he “deserved after such a long and prestigious career”. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Werner Herzog Reveals Orlando Bloom Was Upset On Set Of 'Bucking Fastard' After They Captured His Scene In One Take; Evokes Bond With David Lynch Festivals 'The Girl With The Leica' Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi's Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer - Venice Film Festival The suggestion drew a round of applause from the audience. Malkovich adroitly demured: “I never feel in competition with any of them [actor, director and writer collaborators] because generally I love what they do. The nicest thing is that the film gets attention, and this film has several terrific performers in it, and is beautifully written and beautifully directed, and that’s what matters the most to me. But thank you for your kind words.” Malkovich is considered by prognosticators to be firmly in the mix in what is a very competitive best actor category this awards season with Matt Damon, Tom Cruise, Robert Pattinson, Andrew Scott, Sebastian Stan and Javier Bardem among a deep field. The 72 year-old, who told the audience he has no plans to retire, has two previous Oscar nominations, one in 1985 and one in 1994. After becoming almost a household name in the 80s and 90s, the acclaimed actor hasn’t had the same profile of roles in the past 20 years. There’s little Hollywood loves more than a ‘comeback’. Another journalist in the crowd predicted multiple major awards for the movie. Martin McDonagh has seven Oscar nominations already (and one win). Not many would bet against that number growing. At this stage, at least. Set just before the 1973 Chilean coup, his new film stars Malkovich and Rockwell as CIA agents Chris and Lee, who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island by their bureau chief, MJ (Steve Buscemi). As the longtime partners wrestle with their dark pasts and present conspiracies, Chris’ newfound bond with a pair of rebellious students (Mariana di Girolamo and Ailín Salas) threatens to send everyone’s trip to the remote paradise sideways. Searchlight has set a November 6, 2026 release date for the movie, which also stars Tom Waits. The film marks McDonagh’s first film since The Banshees of Inisherin , which was nominated for nine Oscars in 2023 including for directing, writing and Best Picture. McDonagh and producer Graham Broadbent explained to the press that the film was only the second ever to film on Easter Island/Rapa Nui, something they and the actors described as a great privilege. McDonagh also told the audience that part of his inspiration for telling the story was his fascination with the CIA and the fate of the Chilean government under Salvador Allende. “We know what the KGB are like, but we we probably don’t question the CIA’s activities as much as we ought to,” he said. “That was one of the starting points. I’m always questioning, even in the less less political films [I make]. I like to question authority or what we’re being told.” ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

title: Nicola Coughlan, Luke Evans & Hugh Bonneville Are Speaking Out Against AI Voice Cloning, But Is The Government Listening?
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Jeff Goldblum To Host Season 2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Jasmine Jobson Teases Details About Netflix’s ‘Top Boy’ Spin-Off Series ‘Jaq’: “She’s Going Down A Crazy Rabbit Hole” Maureen Lipman Tells “Cowardly” Co-Star To “Grow Up” After He Quit Play Over Her Pro-Israel Views View All September 3, 2026 5:35am Peter Caulfield, Siobhán McSweeney, and Zawe Ashton support the Save Our Voices Now campaign Save Our Voices Now Welcome to Rendering , a Deadline column reporting at the intersection of AI and showbiz. Rendering examines how artificial intelligence is disrupting the entertainment industry, taking you inside key battlegrounds and spotlighting change-makers wielding the technology for good and ill. Got a story about AI? Rendering wants to hear from you: jkanter@deadline.com. Michael Caine has handed over his voice to AI. Liza Minnelli is making music with AI. With the blessing of their estates, dead actors like John Wayne are having their voices resurrected by AI. But what happens when consent is not given? What can actors do to protect a crucial tool of their craft from unwanted exploitation? The answer, in the UK at least, is very little. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Netflix Sets Roald Dahl Series With Cast Including Nicola Coughlan, Imelda Staunton & Dominic West News Nicola Coughlan On Smaller 'Bridgerton' Season 5 Role Amid 'Only Murders In The Building' Filming: "I Had Such An Epic Run" That’s why Nicola Coughlan , Luke Evans , and Hugh Bonneville are lending their voices to a new campaign: Save Our Voices Now . BAFTA winner Siobhán McSweeney and Harry Potter star Miriam Margolyes have also endorsed the message. The campaign was established by Tip Toe actor Peter Caulfield and Alice Sockett, an established audiobook narrator. They are calling on the government to give individuals enforceable copyright ownership over their own voice. Save Our Voices Now’s Parliament petition has amassed more than 4,000 signatures, but the early indications are that the campaign has been met with inertia rather than action. In December 2024, the British government launched a major consultation on copyright protections in the age of AI. Ministers received 11,520 responses, many of which were from creators and rights holders. The government published the findings of the consultation in March, but said there was no clear consensus on strengthening AI copyright laws, despite 81% of respondents endorsing the need for greater copyright protections. Flash forward five months, and what’s the government’s response to the Save Our Voices Now campaign? To launch another consultation. “It is right that we value and protect human creators, and that is why we have announced we will launch a consultation on how we address these harms, while protecting legitimate innovation,” a Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) spokesperson says. Caulfield is not impressed. “A consultation is such a big fob-off,” he tells Deadline. “We don’t need a second consultation in as many years. We need the law to change.” Actors’ union Equity has also voiced frustration at the government’s position. A DCMS spokesperson did not respond to questions on why a second consultation is necessary and what it will achieve. Meanwhile, the U.S. and Denmark are pushing through legislation that gives citizens the rights to control digital replicas. “The UK is very much lagging behind,” laments Caulfield. “Since we started the campaign, we’ve been inundated with shocking stories about how big brands are taking people’s voices without consent, and AI software is being used to defraud families.” He launched the campaign after submitting audition tapes to Audible, before being “stonewalled” about what was happening to his unsuccessful voice recordings. “They were very reluctant to give me any information about what happens with my data,” he says. Caulfield is not accusing Audible of theft, but is making clear how the rights situation is murky at best. Part of the campaign is about placing the legal burden of consent on the platform and the AI developer, not the individual. But when AI is moving so fast, and legislation is moving so slowly, there are fears it may already be too late. Since launching last week, Save Our Voices Now has attracted further endorsements from Richard E. Grant and The Great British Bake Off presenter Alison Hammond. They will need to speak loudly to make their voices heard in the corridors of power. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Rides Into Awards Race; Mohsen Gharaei; Palestine Call Jeff Goldblum To Host S2 Premiere Of ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Unifrance Rendez-Vous TV Preview & Interview Amid Industry Shifts Scroll Through Photos From Opening Day Of The 83rd Venice Film Festival Read More About: Comments

title: Werner Herzog Reveals Touching Reason Behind ‘Bucking Fastard’ Dedication to David Lynch Ahead of Venice Premiere
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford , Scott Roxborough September 3, 2026 5:29am Domhnall Gleeson, Rooney Mara, Werner Herzog, Kate Mara and Orlando Bloom at the 2026 Venice Film Festival Courtesy of Getty Acclaimed German filmmaker Werner Herzog said he and the late David Lynch “had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work.” Ahead of the Venice Film Festival premiere of Herzog’s latest feature, Bucking Fastard , he sat for a press conference with cast members Kate and Rooney Mara , Domhnall Gleeson and Orlando Bloom . The Fitzcarraldo and Grizzly Man director — who is also picking up the Golden Lion Lifetime Achievement Award on the Lido this year — was swiftly asked why he has dedicated the film to the iconic Lynch ( Blue Velvet , Mulholland Drive , Dune ), who died in January 2025 at the age of 78. Related Stories Lifestyle Jack O'Connell Braves the Venice Heat (and Gets Sweaty) in Dior Look by Jonathan Anderson Movies 'Everest: The Other Side' Review: A Frustrating, Guiltily Compelling Portrait of the Triumph and Tragedy of Extreme Mountaineering He responded: “During editing, I said to the editor just casually, ‘That’s a film that I would like David Lynch to be with me in the first public screening’ — which is in a few hours. […] We had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work, although we were quite different. And I had the feeling [that] I wish he could be my first audience… I wish we could turn the wheel of time back and invite him tonight,” he added with a smile, “but it doesn’t happen like this.” Bucking Fastard follows the Holbrooke sisters, Jean and Joan (the Mara sisters in their first-ever appearance together onscreen), siblings who share a deep, nearly supernatural bond. The sisters dress alike, think alike, and speak simultaneously. They even fall for the same man, the rowdy rogue Gareth Mulroney (Bloom, playing with a thick Irish brogue). Their joint obsession with him leads to legal proceedings and a restraining order. Herzog said that, for the first time, he wasn’t in need of a two-week rehearsal period with his actors. “They were so good instantly that I said, after five days, ‘We stop that. I’ll meet you in Ireland in front of my camera,'” he recalled. “It was complete confidence in them, and they took it with ease.” Rooney Mara said being real-life sisters aided that much-needed synchronicity. “I think we found pretty quickly that having a lifetime together and all this history and a childhood of playing together… There was just an unspoken world between us that we didn’t have to work very hard to create at all,” she told the room. “Once we really found our flow together, I’ve never laughed so much. We had so much fun. it was a very once-in-a-lifetime, unique experience.” Her elder sister added: “Once we figured out the rhythm of our speaking in unison, it felt almost like a song. It was very musical and it happened quite naturally. Surprisingly, it came with a lot of a lot more ease than we were expecting.” The movie is loosely based on the real case of British identical twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, the subjects of a tabloid court case in the 1980s. The film’s title refers to a synchronized verbal slip the sisters made in court. Gleeson plays Timothy, a government-issued social worker who is assigned to the sisters to help them adapt to modern life after the two become tabloid sensations. Gleeson said at Thursday’s presser that it was a little terrifying working with Herzog, and rightly so. “You know that you are in a master’s hands, and so you trust the hands that are holding you,” said the Irish star. “I think it should be scary, and it should feel like a risk every time they call action, or every time Werner does the clapperboard. But you feel safe.” “And also,” he continued, “my experience was the opposite[of] the sisters, and that was an extraordinary thing to witness. It felt like looking between two eyes from the same head, you know? The experience was beautiful. And if [Herzog] asks again, I will say yes.” Herzog’s film takes reality as a jumping-off point. When the sisters decide to “dig a tunnel to an imagined land, where true love is possible,” you quickly become aware you’re in more existential, Herzog-esque territory. The German director has said Bucking Fastard forms an “operatic triptych” alongside 1982’s Fitzcarraldo and 2005’s Grizzly Man , two other works that explore human obsession, isolation and a desire to defy the bounds of nature or society. More surprising perhaps is the tone of the new film, which has more humor and touches of romantic sentimentality, rare, if not completely absent, from Herzog’s large body of work. Herzog reportedly turned down an offer of an out-of-competition slot in Cannes to screen Bucking Fastard in competition in Venice, where it premieres Thursday night and is up for the festival’s Golden Lion. The film was produced by Clara Wu Tsai ( Blue Bayou ), Ariel Leon Isacovitch ( Theater of Thought ), and Agnes Chu ( Spiderhead ), with Kieran Corrigan, Emanuele Moretti and Andrea Bucko. HanWay Films is handling worldwide sales. THR

title: Werner Herzog Reveals Orlando Bloom Was Upset On Set Of ‘Bucking Fastard’ After They Captured His Scene In One Take – Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Sandra Hüller To Star As Celebrated Late Male German Artist Wolfgang Herrndorf’s In Maria Schrader’s ‘Work And Structure’ Calls Grow For Palestinian Flag To Fly At Venice Film Festival As Artistic Director Says Not Possible To Meet Request George Clooney Calls Out “Authoritarians” Who “Peddle Fear” As He Receives Lifetime Award Achievement In Venice View All September 3, 2026 5:15am VENICE, ITALY - SEPTEMBER 03: (L-R) Domhnall Gleeson, Orlando Bloom, Rooney Mara, Kate Mara and Director Werner Herzog attend the "Bucking Fastard" Venice Photocall Getty Images Oscar-nominated German director Werner Herzog set down in Venice Film Festival on Thursday with Golden Lion contender Bucking Fastard , in the company of its stars Kate and Rooney Mara and supporting cast members Domhnall Gleeson and Orlando Bloom . The Maras play Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two real-life sisters who were so close that they spoke in unison, loved the same man, had the same dreams and made the same slips of the tongue. Gleeson plays a man who attempts to help them to adapt to modern life after they become a tabloid sensation, while Bloom plays a rowdy ex-lover. Related Stories Festivals 'The Girl With The Leica' Review: Love Is War In Alina Marazzi's Unconventional Biopic Of A Pioneering War Photographer - Venice Film Festival Festivals Calls Grow For Palestinian Flag To Fly At Venice Film Festival As Artistic Director Says Not Possible To Meet Request Herzog revealed that Lord of the Rings star Bloom had been upset with him after he captured his main scene in just one take. Watch on Deadline “What a pleasure to work with him. He was actually upset because we worked so fast. I did one take of a very long, long thing in the witness stand, and it was that,” said Herzog, addressing Bloom at the press conference. “It was my largest scene in the movie, and we did one take and you said, ‘Great, we got it’,” replied Bloom, explaining his disquiet. Herzog continued that he had understood Bloom’s upset and as a result brought him back to do three more takes. “I do understand you, and I apologize that I was too fast maybe, but it’s the spirit of the film, like open heart surgery, going to the essentials right away. One camera, one take, that’s it. Or maybe two or three takes, with the sister’s highly, highly technically complex.. to speak in unison. Two takes, maybe three takes, and that was that.” Later on in the press conference, Herzog heaped praise on Bloom saying he had been a joy to work with, adding that he had wanted to put the actor in an unexpected role. “I was so much looking forward to work with you, and it came with such natural ease,” said Herzog. “I wanted you to step far out of what you are known for, the heartthrob of teenies. Now you are the ‘Bucking Fastard’. You had to shoulder the title.” Bloom said shooting with Herzog had been liberating and magical. “Werner really creates this sort of sacred space, almost for magic to happen… He has such drive and passion and almost obsession towards making films. And we’ve seen that in everything that he’s done,” said the actor. “ My Best Fiend was a movie I watched with such passion to see the creative process in its finest form,” he continued, referring to the Herzog’s 1990 documentary about his tumultuous friend with Klaus Kinski. “When Werner claps the clapperboard, there’s just a feeling of freedom and because it’s such a small and unique experience, it creates a magical moment. That is what we dream of.” The film is based on the true story of two inseparable sisters living on the fringes of society, whom Herzog first met more than 40 years ago. He said the long gestated project had hit a wall as he grappled with how to capture the two sisters who spoke as one on the big screen. He credited UK producer Jeremy Thomas with coming of the idea of casting Kate and Rooney Mara. “It was dormant for decades, and then when it became clear that I would have actresses who were sisters, it was clear it had to be done. The screenplay came very easily. I wrote it in five days, and it’s a complete invention.” The Maras said that the process of playing the inseparable sisters had come together easily once they were on set because of their strong relationship in real life. “At first it was very daunting the idea that we were going to be kind of playing this same person, but I think we found pretty quickly that having a lifetime together and all this history and you know, a childhood of playing together, there was just an unspoken world between us that we didn’t have to work very hard to create at all,” said Rooney Mara. “Once we found our flow together… you know, I’ve never laughed so much. We had so much fun and yeah, it was a very once in a lifetime, very unique experience.” Venice regular Herzog was at the festival last year to receive its Golden Lion Life Achievement Award from Francis Coppola, who has been his friend since he time spent in L.A. in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Ahead of tonight’s world premiere, Herzog expressed regrets that another old friend from L.A., David Lynch, who died in January 2025, would not be in the audience. “We had a deep, deep understanding of each other’s work, although we were quite different… I had the feeling I wish he could be my first audience… I wish we could turn the wheel of time back and invite him tonight. title: Jack O’Connell Braves the Venice Heat (and Gets Sweaty) in Dior Look by Jonathan Anderson
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 3, 2026 5:15am Jack O'Connell attends Netflix's 'Ink' screening during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Sala Grande on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Aurore Marechal/Getty Images) Who says men don’t suffer for fashion, too? Jack O’Connell showed himself to be a man of extremes at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. The veteran English actor hit the Lido for the world premiere of his new Danny Boyle film from Netflix, Ink , by dressing for multiple seasons in a matter of hours, styled by Luke Day. First, O’Connell turned up at Palazzo del Casino for an afternoon press conference and photocall alongside his Ink team — Boyle, Claire Foy , Guy Pearce and the filmmaking and Netflix teams — wearing a simple white Henley paired with black trousers. Related Stories Movies 'Eklipse' Mixes the Autobiographical and Fictional to Explore AIDS Taboos and Fear of Social Exclusion Movies 'Queer Edward II' Takes Us Behind the Scenes of Derek Jarman's Film Shoot and a Political Backlash (Exclusive Venice Clip) O’Connell attends Netflix’s ‘Ink’ photocall at Palazzo del Casino on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Kate Green/Getty Images for Netflix) For the evening world premiere, O’Connell stepped out of his car to hit the red carpet for the opening ceremony wearing a white tuxedo shirt and bow tie with trousers by Dior. Before stepping onto the red carpet to face the crush of photographers, O’Connell’s rep slipped him into a summer stunner: a gray wool overcoat with tuxedo lapels and an ankle-length scarf over his shoulders by Jonathan Anderson for Dior. The coat comes from Anderson’s spring/summer 2027 collection for Dior, so maybe it wasn’t a surprise to some, however, the Venice Film Festival happens at a time in September that typically delivers sweltering heat and humidity. Wednesday’s temperature reached a high of 87 degrees and a low of 70, so not quite as bad as it could’ve been but still pretty sweaty. And O’Connell was not immune. After making his way down the red carpet in front of photographers, he slipped back out of the coat before making his way down to the barricade to greet a long line of adoring fans, some of whom had been camped out there overnight to see the parade of stars on opening night. In addition to Ink , the ceremony featured a lifetime achievement award presentation to George Clooney. O’Connell in Dior at Netflix’s Ink screening at Sala Grande on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) After O’Connell finished signing autographs and posing for selfies, he made his way back up towards the entrance, where he took a cloth to dab all the sweat off his forehead and face (groomed by Brady Lea) while a rep helped him fix his bow tie. During the screening, O’Connell left the overcoat off and opted to wear just the long scarf, which could be seen over his shoulders amid the film’s four-minute standing ovation. Venice’s iconic red carpet can be a challenge for stylists. Actors want to look glamorous for their premieres, yet the heat and humidity are always a factor. Though some just choose to brave the high temperatures and go for a great photo opportunity over something light and airy for the weather. Case in point: A few years back, Angelina Jolie wore a faux fur stole for the Venice premiere of Pablo Larrain’s Maria during an epic heatwave in Italy that week. Back to O’Connell. Ink finds the Sinners star playing ruthless tabloid editor Larry Lamb in Boyle’s retelling of what happened when Rupert Murdoch acquired struggling British newspaper The Sun . Murdoch, played by Pearce, recruited Lamb to reinvent it as a populist tabloid capable of overtaking the dominant Daily Mirror. The film traces the creation of a formula built around sensationalism, celebrity, sex and an instinctive feel for readers’ baser instincts — an approach that would transform The Sun into Britain’s bestselling newspaper and presage many of the forces that later reshaped global media. Ink is screening in competition in Venice. The film will release in select theaters in the U.S. on Dec. 11 before going out on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America. title: How Rooney and Kate Mara Learned to Speak in Unison for Werner Herzog’s ‘Bucking Fastard’: ‘It Happened Quite Naturally’
